scenarios.title: Entrepreneurship as a discipline
scenarios.situation: A friend says entrepreneurs are born, not made — 'you either have the risk gene or you don't.' You're studying a curriculum that treats entrepreneurship the way business schools treat finance or marketing: a teachable body of method. Your friend challenges you: if it's teachable, why do most startups still fail?
choices: Entrepreneurship is a method — a repeatable process for discovering problems, testing solutions, and managing uncertainty — and a teachable method still fails often because it operates under irreducible uncertainty: the method improves your odds and your cost per experiment, it doesn't remove risk.
Your friend is right; the curriculum is just motivational speaking with tuition attached.
Most startups fail because founders didn't take enough risk; the method says to bet bigger.
The method guarantees success if followed exactly; failures come from skipping steps.
scenarios.why: Treating entrepreneurship as a discipline means there are learnable skills — customer discovery, unit economics, MVP design — that separate deliberate founders from gamblers. But the domain is uncertainty itself: even perfect method leaves market risk, timing risk, and competition. The discipline's promise is cheaper, faster, more informative failures — more at-bats per dollar — not certainty.
scenarios.hint: Does a good batting coach guarantee every hit?

scenarios.title: The foundations audit
scenarios.situation: You've built a prototype people like, but every business conversation exposes a gap: you can't read the P&L a potential partner sends, your 'marketing plan' is 'post on social media,' and you have no idea what fulfilling 1,000 orders would actually cost. A mentor says to pause and audit your foundations.
scenarios.prompt: What does the foundations audit cover, and why does it come before scaling the prototype?
choices: Finance (can you read statements and model cash), marketing (do you know your customer, channel, and message), and operations (can you deliver at volume, at cost) — because a beloved prototype with broken foundations scales losses, not a business.
It covers pitch-deck design, logo refinement, and social media growth hacks.
It covers finding a technical co-founder; everything else can be outsourced later.
Foundations don't matter until Series A; early stage is only about the product.
scenarios.why: The three foundations map to the three ways startups die after product-market fit: they run out of cash (finance), they can't acquire customers repeatably (marketing), or they can't deliver what they sold (operations). Auditing them before scaling is triage: each gap has a learn-or-hire answer, but an unaudited gap becomes the company's cause of death.
scenarios.hint: Which of the three foundations kills the company if the prototype succeeds?

scenarios.title: Problem discovery before product
scenarios.situation: A founder has spent four months building an app for restaurant scheduling. They've spoken to zero restaurant managers. When you suggest customer interviews, they say 'I already know the problem — I worked in a restaurant in college' and 'talking to people will just slow me down.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the specific failure mode here, and what should happen instead?
choices: Solution-first building on an unvalidated problem: four months of engineering on an assumed pain. The fix is problem discovery — structured interviews with the actual buyers to learn whether the pain is real, urgent, and budgeted — before writing more code.
The failure is not building fast enough; they should add features to differentiate.
The failure is not having a co-founder; solo founders can't do discovery.
Interviews are fine but the real validation is a bigger launch with more users.
scenarios.why: Working in a restaurant gave them a hypothesis, not evidence. Problem discovery interviews test whether the pain is frequent, expensive, and owned by someone with budget — the three properties that make a problem worth solving. Code is the most expensive way to test a hypothesis; conversations are the cheapest. The MVP discipline starts by refusing to build until the problem earns it.
scenarios.hint: What three properties make a customer problem worth building for?

scenarios.title: The unit economics trap
scenarios.situation: A subscription startup celebrates: 10,000 users, growing 20% monthly, 'profitable on paper' because this month's revenue finally exceeded this month's ad spend. You look closer: customer acquisition cost is $60, average customer lifetime is 4 months at $10/month margin, and churn is accelerating.
scenarios.prompt: What is the real unit economics verdict?
choices: The business loses money on every customer: lifetime value is 4 × $10 = $40 against a $60 acquisition cost — LTV/CAC is 0.67, below the 1.0 breakeven and far below the 3.0 healthy threshold. Growth is scaling losses; the celebration is premature.
It's profitable: revenue exceeded ad spend this month, which is the definition of profitability.
The 20% growth rate compensates; unit economics don't matter at this stage.
Churn doesn't matter as long as new users keep arriving faster.
scenarios.why: Unit economics ask one question: does one customer, over their whole lifetime, pay back what they cost to acquire? LTV = $40, CAC = $60, so each new customer destroys $20 of value and 20% growth just destroys it faster. 'Revenue beat ad spend this month' confuses a single month's cash timing with the lifetime math. Fix churn or CAC before spending another dollar on growth.
scenarios.hint: Compute LTV from the numbers given. Is it above or below CAC?

scenarios.title: Reading the term sheet
scenarios.situation: After a long fundraise, you receive your first term sheet: a $2M raise on an $8M pre-money valuation, with a 1x liquidation preference, pro-rata rights for the investor, and a board seat. Your co-founder says 'valuation is all that matters — $8M pre is great, sign it.'
scenarios.prompt: What should you actually evaluate before signing?
choices: The full economics and control package: your post-money ownership ($2M on $8M pre = 20% dilution before option pool), what the 1x liquidation preference means in a modest exit, the option pool shuffle (whose shares fund the employee pool), board control, and protective provisions — valuation is one term among many that determine what you actually keep and control.
Valuation only; the other terms are standard boilerplate that never matters.
Only the board seat matters; economics sort themselves out.
Reject it; any dilution above 10% is unacceptable at this stage.
scenarios.why: A $2M raise on $8M pre-money means you sell 20% of the company — and the option pool, typically topped up pre-money, comes out of the founders' share, not the investors'. The 1x liquidation preference decides who gets paid first in a $5M exit (not you, fully). Fundraising literacy means reading every term as dilution, downside protection, or control — then negotiating the package, not the headline number.
scenarios.hint: If the company sells for $5M, who gets paid first under a 1x preference?

scenarios.title: Borrowing from practitioner models
scenarios.situation: You're accepted to a practitioner-led founder program modeled on the contemporary academy approach: operators teach, the curriculum centers on AI-era building, and hiring partners recruit from graduates. The cost is 6% equity. A friend says 'never give up equity for education' — but your alternative is learning alone for a year.
scenarios.prompt: How do you evaluate the offer?
choices: Price the 6% against the specific, verifiable value: the instructors' operating track records, the hiring partners' actual placement rates, the curriculum's relevance to what you're building, and your opportunity cost of a solo year — take it only if the expected acceleration exceeds 6% of the company's eventual value, and verify every claim before signing.
Always take it; networks are everything and equity is free at this stage.
Never take it; equity is the most expensive currency and education should be free.
Decide based on the program's marketing and demo-day hype videos.
scenarios.why: Practitioner-led education can compress years of mistakes into months — but 6% of a successful company is an enormous tuition. The evaluation is arithmetic plus diligence: expected value of acceleration (faster to revenue, better hires, fewer fatal mistakes) versus 6% of terminal value, with every placement and instructor claim verified against graduate outcomes, not brochures. 'What to borrow, what to avoid' is a due-diligence question, not an ideology.
scenarios.hint: What would the 6% be worth if the company exits at $50M?

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track — Core concepts
concepts: Entrepreneurship is a discipline, not a personality trait: a teachable method for discovering valuable problems and building solutions under uncertainty. The method improves your cost per experiment and your odds; it does not remove risk.

The foundations audit comes before scale: finance (read statements, model cash, understand runway), marketing (know the customer, the channel, the message), operations (deliver at volume, at cost). Beloved prototypes with broken foundations scale losses.

Problem discovery precedes product: structured customer interviews establish whether a pain is real, frequent, expensive, and budgeted — code is the most expensive hypothesis test, conversation the cheapest.

The MVP discipline: the minimum viable product is the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption. Concierge, Wizard-of-Oz, and landing-page MVPs validate demand before engineering validates the build.

Unit economics are the verdict on the business model: LTV must exceed CAC (healthy: 3:1), payback periods must fit your cash, and contribution margin must survive scale. Growth on broken unit economics is just faster losses.

Fundraising literacy: valuation is one term among many — dilution, liquidation preference, option pool, board control, and protective provisions determine what founders actually keep. Price practitioner programs (equity, time, cash) against verified acceleration, not marketing.

example.walkthrough: Lifetime is the reciprocal of monthly churn (4 months at 25% churn); LTV is monthly contribution margin times lifetime. The scenario's startup prints LTV/CAC = 0.67 — BROKEN — which is the arithmetic behind the scenario's verdict: each customer destroys $20. Change churn to 8% and watch the verdict flip; that sensitivity is the whole strategy conversation.

pitfalls: Common trap: building before discovering. Months of engineering on an assumed problem is the most expensive possible way to learn the problem wasn't real — interview first.
Common trap: confusing revenue with unit economics. A month where revenue beats ad spend says nothing about whether each customer pays back their acquisition cost over their lifetime.
Common trap: negotiating valuation instead of the term sheet. Dilution, liquidation preference, and the option pool shuffle determine founder outcomes more than the headline pre-money number.
Common trap: treating programs and accelerators as ideology. Price every offer — equity, time, cash — against verified acceleration for your specific company, not demo-day footage.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Unit economics verdict engine
labs.objective: Extend the lesson's unit-economics function into a script that evaluates three pricing scenarios for a hypothetical startup and prints which (if any) is fundable on unit economics alone.
steps: Create economics.py with the unit_economics function from the lesson.
Define three scenarios: (A) the broken baseline (CAC 60, ARPU 10, churn 25%), (B) improved retention (churn 8%), (C) premium pricing (ARPU 25, CAC 90, churn 10%).
Print each scenario's LTV, LTV/CAC, payback months, and verdict.
Add a sensitivity line: for scenario B, print how the verdict changes if CAC rises 50%.
Write the one-paragraph investment memo in RESULTS.txt: which scenario would you fund and what single metric would you watch weekly.

checks.hint: Scenario A should print the BROKEN verdict.
At least one improved scenario should reach HEALTHY.

labs.title: Problem-discovery interview plan
labs.objective: Write a structured problem-discovery interview guide and a riskiest-assumption MVP proposal for a startup idea of your choice — the two documents the MVP discipline requires before code.
steps: Create discovery.md: 8 interview questions that uncover problem frequency, cost, current workarounds, and budget ownership — no questions about your solution allowed.
Add a 'listening rules' section: the interviewer talks 20% of the time, no pitching, record exact customer language.
Create mvp.md: name the single riskiest assumption, then design the smallest test for it (concierge, landing page, or Wizard-of-Oz) with a falsifiable pass/fail criterion.
Add the kill criteria: what result would make you abandon or pivot the idea.
Print both files to the terminal to review them as a founder would before a build decision.

checks.hint: Your interview guide must probe budget ownership.
Name the riskiest assumption explicitly in mvp.md.

sections.title: Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track — Core path

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you identified a real customer problem — not one you assumed.
points: Describe the discovery method: who you talked to, what you asked, what surprised you
Show the evidence that the problem was real: frequency, cost, workarounds, budget
Explain what you built or changed because of what you learned
pitfalls: A problem you never validated with actual customers
Skipping the surprise — discovery without surprise is confirmation bias
No link between the learning and the action

behavioral.prompt: Describe your biggest failure as a builder or founder and what it taught you.
points: Own the failure plainly: what you did, what it cost in time or money
Name the specific mistake in method (skipped discovery, ignored unit economics, scaled too early)
Show the changed behavior: what you do differently now, with an example
pitfalls: A humblebrag failure with no real cost
Blaming the market, the team, or timing
No demonstrated change in method

behavioral.prompt: Walk me through how you'd validate a startup idea in two weeks with $500.
points: Start with the riskiest assumption and the cheapest test for it
Show the weekly cadence: interviews, landing page, concierge MVP, metrics
Name the kill criteria: what evidence would make you stop
pitfalls: Spending the $500 on logo and incorporation
No falsifiable criteria
Two weeks of building with no customer contact

behavioral.prompt: Explain unit economics to a non-technical co-founder in two minutes.
points: Use a single concrete customer: what they cost to acquire, what they pay over their lifetime
State the verdict rule plainly: LTV must beat CAC, 3-to-1 is healthy
Connect it to their decisions: why this governs how fast you can grow
pitfalls: Jargon without the example
No verdict rule given
Longer than two minutes

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a disagreement with a co-founder or partner and how you resolved it.
points: Describe the disagreement on its merits, fairly representing their side
Show the resolution mechanism: data, customer evidence, or a reversible experiment — not authority
Name what the partnership learned about deciding together
pitfalls: Painting the other person as irrational
Resolving by fiat or by who cared more
No mechanism for the next disagreement

behavioral.prompt: Why do you want to be a founder instead of joining a great team?
points: Give the real reason: the specific problem you can't not work on, or the craft you want to own end-to-end
Show you understand the trade: lower pay, higher variance, total accountability
Demonstrate founder traits with evidence: shipped things, recruited people, survived uncertainty
pitfalls: 'Be my own boss' as the whole answer
No evidence of building anything
Ignoring the downside of the trade

behavioral.prompt: Pitch your startup idea in 60 seconds.
points: Problem: who hurts, how often, what it costs them — in one sentence
Solution: what you do differently, in one sentence
Proof: the strongest evidence you have (users, revenue, LOIs)
Ask: what you want from this listener, specifically
pitfalls: Leading with features instead of the problem
No proof offered
No ask at the end

behavioral.prompt: What would you do if your startup's unit economics turned out to be broken after launch?
points: Show the diagnostic: which lever — CAC, churn, pricing, margin — is actually broken, with numbers
Sequence the fixes by cost and reversibility: pricing tests before rebuilds
Name the shutdown criterion: when you'd stop rather than burn more capital
pitfalls: 'Raise more money to grow through it'
No diagnostic — jumping to a fix
No willingness to consider shutting down

cheatsheet.title: Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track — field reference

sections.heading: The discipline
items: Entrepreneurship = method for discovering problems and testing solutions under uncertainty
Method improves cost-per-experiment and odds; it does not remove risk
Foundations audit: finance, marketing, operations — before scale

sections.heading: Venture building
items: Problem discovery: real, frequent, expensive, budgeted — interviews before code
MVP: smallest test of the riskiest assumption; concierge / Wizard-of-Oz / landing page
Kill criteria decided in advance; pivots are data-driven, not emotional

sections.heading: Unit economics
items: LTV = ARPU x gross margin / churn; healthy LTV/CAC >= 3
Growth on broken unit economics scales losses

sections.heading: Fundraising literacy
items: Dilution = raise / post-money; option pool usually comes from founders
1x liquidation preference: investors paid first in a modest exit
Negotiate the package (dilution, control, downside), not just valuation

glossary.def: Structured customer research establishing that a pain is real, frequent, expensive, and budgeted — done before building.
Minimum viable product: the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption, not a stripped-down version of the vision.
The per-customer profit math: lifetime value versus acquisition cost, payback period, and contribution margin.
Lifetime value divided by customer acquisition cost; below 1.0 the business loses money per customer, 3.0+ is healthy.
A term-sheet provision paying investors back (typically 1x their investment) before common shareholders in an exit.
The practice of topping up the employee option pool pre-money, so the dilution comes from founders' shares rather than investors'.
Programs taught by working operators rather than academics, trading theory for current field practice.
Pre-committed evidence thresholds that trigger abandoning or pivoting an idea — decided before emotional attachment sets in.
